plan: Informative essay (CLD-P-ACT-E-000050) on David Brewster's kaleidoscope: discovery while studying light, the name, the flawed patent, mass copying, and lost profits. Sales stated only as 'an enormous number'. Topic checked against every bank (no matches). Eight new items, three aimed at hard (conjunctive adverb, 'a number of' agreement, phrase-deletion effect). Plus E049-07 resubmitted as revision 2 on banked passage CLD-P-ACT-E-000049 (choice A narrowed so it is clearly false). Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Beautiful Forms
A Better Way to Fasten Boots
passages.text:
[1] In 1893, an inventor named Whitcomb Judson patented a device he called a "clasp locker." [2] It was meant to replace the long rows of buttons and hooks on high boots, {{1|but it had a serious flaw: it}} tended to pop open without warning.

[3] The problem was solved two decades later by Gideon Sundback, a Swedish-born engineer working for the company that had acquired Judson's patents. [4] {{2|Sundback's design, which used}} rows of small interlocking teeth, each shaped with a small bump on top and a matching hollow underneath. [5] A slider pressed the teeth together so that each bump nested inside the hollow of the tooth above it. [6] {{4|Increasing the number of teeth per inch, the fastener became both smaller and far more secure.}}

[7] Sundback called his invention the "hookless fastener," a name that {{5|did little to excite}} customers. [8] Sales stayed modest until 1923, when the B. F. Goodrich Company used it on a line of rubber boots. {{10|}} [9] The company's president is said to have enjoyed the sound the boots made as they were closed{{6| and he decided to call}} them "Zippers." [10] Before long, the name had spread from the boots to the fastener itself.

[11] Today, zippers close everything from jackets to tents to suitcases. [12] {{8|Few of the people who use them every day knows}} that the device began as a better way to fasten boots.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: The subject of the clause is "objects," which is plural, so the verb must be "were." The phrase "between them" does not change the subject.

A.rationale: The subject is the plural "objects," so the singular "was" does not agree.

C.rationale: The comma wrongly separates the subject from the verb, and "was" still does not agree with "objects."

D.rationale: "Repeating" leaves the clause after "that" without a main verb.

hints: What is the subject of the verb in the "that" clause?
candidates.remember: A prepositional phrase does not change the number of the subject.

candidates.subskill: Parallel structure in a series of verbs
candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: added colored glass at one end and,
choices.C: added colored glass at one end, and
choices.D: colored glass was added at one end, and

candidates.evidence: Brewster built a tube around the mirrors
candidates.explanation: The sentence lists three actions by Brewster: built, added, and called. All three should be past-tense verbs.

A.rationale: "Adding" breaks the series of past-tense verbs "built ... and called."

B.rationale: The comma belongs before "and," not after it.

D.rationale: This shifts to the passive voice and breaks the parallel series of actions by Brewster.

hints: What other verbs are in the series?

strategy.explanation: Match the form of each item in the series.

candidates.remember: Items in a series should share the same grammatical form.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: Brewster patented the device in 1817 however his patent
choices.C: Brewster patented the device in 1817; however his patent,
choices.D: Brewster patented the device in 1817; however, his patent

candidates.explanation: "However" joins two independent clauses, so it needs a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

A.rationale: A comma before "however" creates a comma splice between two independent clauses.

B.rationale: Without punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

C.rationale: The comma after "patent" wrongly separates the subject from its verb "had."

hints: Can "however" join two sentences with just commas?

strategy.explanation: Check each version for a splice or a stray comma.

candidates.remember: Use a semicolon before a conjunctive adverb that joins two independent clauses.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: "Almost immediately" expresses the timing once, with no repetition.

B.rationale: "Immediately" and "right away" mean the same thing.

hints: Do any choices repeat an idea?

strategy.explanation: Pick the shortest choice that keeps the meaning.

candidates.remember: When choices mean the same thing, the shortest clear one is best.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: Within months, an enormous number of
candidates.explanation: "A number of" + plural noun takes a plural verb because it means "many," so "were sold" is correct.

A.rationale: "An enormous number of kaleidoscopes" refers to many kaleidoscopes, so a plural verb is needed.

C.rationale: "Has" is singular, and the present perfect does not fit a past event.

hints: Does "an enormous number of kaleidoscopes" mean one thing or many?

strategy.explanation: Decide whether the phrase means many items.

candidates.remember: "A number of" takes a plural verb; "the number of" takes a singular one.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: "However" interrupts the subject and verb, so it is set off with commas on both sides.

A.rationale: "However" interrupts the sentence, so it needs a comma on each side.

B.rationale: A semicolon cannot separate the subject "Brewster" from its verb.

D.rationale: A comma is needed after "Brewster" to open the interruption.

candidates.remember: An interrupting word needs commas on both sides.

candidates.stem:
At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence:
Modern kaleidoscopes are sometimes built with three or more mirrors instead of two.
Should the writer make this addition here?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains why copies of Brewster's design appeared in shops so quickly.
choices.B: Yes, because it shows that Brewster's original design was later improved by others.
choices.C: No, because it contradicts the earlier statement that Brewster used two mirrors.
choices.D: No, because it moves from Brewster's patent trouble to a detail about modern designs.

candidates.evidence: Brewster, however earned little from them.
candidates.explanation: The paragraph is about the patent problem and Brewster's lost profits; a detail about modern mirror arrangements is off topic.

A.rationale: The sentence does not explain the copies; it describes modern designs.

B.rationale: Even if true, this does not fit the paragraph's focus on Brewster's lost profits.

C.rationale: The sentence describes modern devices; it does not contradict Brewster's design.

strategy.explanation: State the focus, then test the sentence.

candidates.remember: Add a sentence only if it supports the paragraph's focus.

candidates.stem: If the writer were to delete the underlined portion (ending the sentence with a period after the word toy), the essay would primarily lose:

choices.A: information suggesting Brewster saw practical uses for his invention.
choices.B: an explanation of how the mirrors in a kaleidoscope create patterns.
choices.C: a detail showing that Brewster earned money by selling to artists.
choices.D: a contrast between Brewster's scientific research and his invention.

candidates.evidence: remembered less for that research than for a toy
candidates.explanation: The phrase tells the reader that Brewster hoped the kaleidoscope would help artists and designers, a practical purpose beyond being a toy.

B.rationale: The explanation of the mirrors is in sentence 2, not this phrase.

C.rationale: The phrase describes a hope, not earnings; sentence 7 says he earned little.

D.rationale: The contrast is made by "less for that research than for a toy," which remains after the deletion.

hints: What does the phrase add about Brewster's view of the device?

strategy.explanation: Ask what would be missing without the phrase.

candidates.remember: Judge a phrase by what the reader would not know without it.

candidates.subskill: Evaluating whether an essay meets a goal
candidates.stem: Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to explain how a product came to have its name. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?

choices.A: Yes, because it is mainly about how the fastener's name changed from product to product.
choices.B: Yes, because it describes in detail the interlocking teeth that made the fastener secure.
choices.C: No, because it never explains where the word "zipper" came from in the first place.
choices.D: No, because it explains the name only briefly and focuses mainly on developing the fastener.

candidates.evidence: Before long, the name had spread from the boots to the fastener itself.
candidates.explanation: The naming story occupies only two sentences; most of the essay describes Judson's device and Sundback's design, so the essay does not have naming as its primary purpose.

A.rationale: The naming story takes up only two sentences; most of the essay is about the invention.

B.rationale: Describing the teeth does not explain how the product got its name.

C.rationale: Sentences 9 and 10 explain where the word came from.

hints: How much of the essay is about the name?

strategy.explanation: Compare the goal with the essay's main focus, then check each reason.

candidates.remember: An essay meets a purpose only if that purpose is its main focus.

revision_history.reason: solvers: choice A (true but partial) was somewhat defensible; A now claims the essay is mainly about the name, which is clearly false
